Police Suicides

By: Busisiwe Gumede | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Police murder-suicide reveals South Africa’s dark underbelly, a problem that experts say needs urgent solutions.

Unique Selling Point:
We zoom into police suicides in the country. Many of these cases highlight the all-to-familiar but unrecognised story about our country’s masculinity, violence and mental health that is playing out in the context of policing. We will be speaking to families who have lost, survivors and experts in the field.


Summary:
We look at two recent cases where policeman killed their partners before turning the gun on themselves. Kgothatso was killed by her policeman love at the tembisa hospital where she worked. in 2010, Katlego survived a near death event, after her ex-boyfriend shot her partner in front of their child. She fortunately had gone to the shops nearby. She returned to a devastating sight of her dead boyfriend. What dies this tell us about the mental health of policemen in our country? POPCRU says it has all the answers. The union says the police are exposed to gruesome cases every single day and they do not get enough help to unpack them. But is there a direct link between work and their actions? We interview a psychologist who breaks it down.

Press Release:


Police Suffering in Silence

Policing the third most dangerous country in the world exacts a heavy mental and emotional toll. With poor salaries and a lack of promotion prospects within the South African Police Service suicide rates are high – over 40 cases in the last two years. Carte Blanche tells the stories of police officers dealing with post-traumatic stress that undermines their ability to work, and dying by suicide, often taking the lives of loved ones in the process. Is enough being done to make mental health support accessible?

Producer: Busisiwe Gumede-Chizhanje | Presenter: Claire Mawisa

Script:


VO - Sirens and blue lights - the call of duty for police officers sworn to serve and protect. But for some, a call-out from which they may never return.
In a country ranked the world’s third most dangerous,our policemen and women are overworked and often overwhelmed. It’s been that way for a LONG time.

ANONYMOUS COP My whole family was in the police force, my dad, my uncles. At the time, this was in 1979 when I joined the force.

VO - The workload has always been excessive - complicated by extreme and brutal cases. This retired officer doesn’t want to reveal his identity…

ANONYMOUS COP 12:13 - I was tasked with picking up bodies. I worked at the SCI and every day, I picked up bodies. And so it just messed up my life completely. I couldn’t live a normal life. 02:02 - It affected my personal life. My family life. I was married and my marriage ended in divorce. And I became an alcoholic so to speak. If you were going for psychological help then you were referred to as a weakling. You couldn’t take the pressure, you couldn’t take the job.

VO – He was medically boarded in 2001 with post traumatic stress disorder so severe, it impacted his ability to work. A common theme in the police.

This mental anguish - and the determination to suffer in silence - raises a critical question: could it be the reason some officers respond so violently to stress in their personal lives?
In February, 30-year old Lebohang Monene was at Tembisa Hospital where she worked as a nursing assistant. The father of her young son called her from the parking lot. They had a stormy relationship…and that day, a big argument.
Lebohang’s father, Malesela Monene got the devastating call.

MASELELA MONENE - They said Lebo was shot. I asked who did it. They said it’s the man she was living with. I fell off my chair when they told me.

VO - That man was an officer of the law.

MASELELA MONENE - This guy had previously threatened Lebo with a gun. Saying he’ll shoot her if he left the relationship.

VO – And, according to her childhood friend, Lina Mogwawa, Lebohang had every reason to leave.

LINA MOKGOWA 03:40 - Imagine beating her inside a mall in front of everyone, a policeman. Imagine. That is why it was easy for him to shoot her right inside of a public hospital.

VO – Unlike Lebohang, Paballo Mosunkutu didn't report her abusive police officer boyfriend because she feared he would respond with more violence.

PABALLO MOSUNKUTU - He would hit me, some of the days. He would talk to me in a rough way. We didn’t agree to break up, I just left because I realised that it’s too much for me.

VO - In 2016 Paballo wasn’t home when Officer John Mabuza called round to drop off their 4-year old son. She’d left him months earlier and was now with a new boyfriend, Dan Phasha. That day the two men came face to face.

05:44 - Dan called me and said John is here to drop off the child. Knowing how violent John was, I came running. Then I heard “twah-twah”. When I arrived I found Dan laying on the street and John ran back into his car.

VO – In the chaos of Dan's killing, Paballo didn't immediately realise that John had not been alone in the car.

PABALLO MOSUNKUTU - My son Katlego was four years old when it happened. He said John asked him to untie his shoelaces. Then John shot himself as Katlego was untying his shoe laces. Then he fell on the child.

John would come to the house, while I’m asleep in that other bedroom and I’d see him pass the window holding a gun. 11:34 - like he would peep into the window, and I’d open it and ask what he wants. ... Then he would leave.

VO – Paballo thinks she can pin-point the time John turned from a loving, protective partner to a jealous, violent monster.

PABALLO MOSUNKUTU - When I looked through John’s Facebook I realised, that John wasn’t happy with his job, like he was complaining.

CLAIRE LINK - Homocide-suicide is an act in which an individual kills one or more people before killing themself. Many studies suggest the phenomenon appears to be increasing among members of the South African Police Service. This is because they are constantly exposed to stressful decision-making situations, serious injury and death on the job.
A 2009 study by the University of Pretoria shows the biggest proportion of intimate partner homicide-suicide perpetrators are police members.. with 90% of the victims female.
VO – The Pretoria University study notes that cases of suicide that follow the murder of an intimate partner are often linked to relationship turmoil.
It’s a view supported by forensic psychologist and veteran of the police service Dr Gerard Labuschagne. He believes its a mistake to see homicide-suicides as purely the result of job pressures.
GÉRARD LABUSCHAGNE – FORENSIC PSYCHOLOGIST – CLIP 003
14:28 - ... It’s a domestic violence issue. 14:44 - ... That is the same context that when this happens outside the police. So you almost always find that there is a pattern or background of domestic violence. There is controlling behavior, jealous behavior. Not wanting to accept the relationship is ending. I don’t know if it’s fair to automatically assume that it's the job. You find people working in logistics who committed suicide. We will always have people who end up committing suicide no matter what occupation they are in. No matter how wonderful their lives are going.
VO - But still - the numbers appear to be mounting.

LINK - In theory the SAPS offers significant aid to its members via its Employee Health and Wellness Service. Their programs include anger management and domestic violence just to name a few. But there doesn’t appear to be a national standard for treatment or even data to determine the scale of the problem.

VO – Almost eighty per cent of the police service received proactive training on anger management and domestic violence in 2018. A little under 35 000 sought assistance from the in-house employee wellness service with benefits like trauma counseling.
It’s unlikely these figures accurately reflect the extent of the mental health problem within police ranks – many choose to suffer in silence.

RICHARD MAMABOLO - Now if you have been through those processes and your information leaks that you had PTSD for example, it then means that the seniors who have to interview you, who assess you before getting promoted, would have a view about you already, so that is seen as a disadvantage for most members.

VO - But if every officer needing trauma therapy requested it, the police service simply wouldn’t be equipped to meet the demand.

RICHARD MAMABOLO
Currently those services utilise the services of social workers and priests. 26:42 - The social workers are limited of course, there aren’t enough.
Claire: Priests?
Mamabolo : Yes priests, hallelujah…
Claire - Wow.

VO - While it’s not unusual for priests to counsel police officers, it’s unlikely they possess the professional skills needed to deal with complex psychological issues. But that’s a criticism not limited to people of the cloth.

GÉRARD LABUSCHAGNE - So what SAPS did to try and rectify that, which is wrong, is they started to employ people who weren’t qualified registered psychologists with the Health Professions Council.

Claire 26:19 Shouldn’t it then be compulsory requirement

26:24 ideally it should however the one challenge is there is a lack of capacity.
26:42 the social workers are limited of course they aren’t enough. That’s why they cannot be everywhere at the same time

VO - THE SHORTAGES OF PROPERLY QUALIFIED STAFF ASIDE, THE IMPLICATIONS OF ARMED POLICE OFFICERS WITH UNTREATED PSYCHOLOGICAL DAGAMES ARE SERIOUS. HAS THE TIME COME FOR THE SAPS TO TALE A TOUGHER STANCE ON TREATMENT?

VO - Our numerous requests for an interview with the police went unanswered. Nor could we check official statistics…or suitability of support services to members with depression and post-traumatic stress.

LINA MOKGOWA 00:34 – Eish, losing Lebo, looking at her children and asking ourselves, how will they grow up knowing that someone killed their mother? 04:11 - How do you shoot your own mother of your own son? How do you do this?

VO – Questions they hope will be answered when the suspect is able to appear in court. His attempt to take his own life failed, and he’s currently recovering in hospital.

MASELELA MONENE 23:09 - It really hurt my feelings. I couldn’t believe it. 23:46 - I struggled to raise these kids that’s why my heart is so sore.
